We believe that is projected to grow to $6.4 trillion annually by 2030. Africa alone faces a shortfall of $1.6 trillion per year. While half of all new greenfield investment now targets green and digital sectors, the jobs generated per dollar invested have actually fallen by 17%. These numbers make one thing clear. We don't just need more investment, we need better investment. Investment that creates jobs, investment that drives inclusion, investment that powers the green and digital transformation. That is why quality investment is our focus, and that is what we are focusing on here today in the mobilization effort. The question before us is clear. Why are the vast savings, both within Africa and globally, not flowing to meet the continent's immense investment needs and opportunities? One part of that answer is risk, whether that risk is real or perceived. These risks drive up the cost of capital and make investment in Africa less competitive. So why the Africa Virtual Investment Platform? AVIP stands as an important tool to attract more quality investment to the African countries. Through AVIP, we want to achieve the following objectives. Bridge the information gaps. by providing more granular and regularly updated indicators on domestic and foreign investment, infrastructure, ecosystems, and policy settings. Secondly, to align the risk perceptions with reality, showcasing investment opportunities while flagging the reform priorities that individual countries are focused on. Thirdly, catalyzing cooperation. through peer learning and capacity building with national governments, statistical offices, and regional economic communities. One core part of the platform will focus on tracking the real impact of investment on jobs, on skills, on digital transformation, on gender equality, and on climate goals. This draws on the OECD's FDI Qualities Framework. I'm also very pleased to share that this week marks the global launch of our new FDI Qualities Visualization Platform. This is part of the SEVIA Platform for Action initiatives. This strong backing reflects the international community's clear and growing commitment to Africa's investment solutions. We are aiming to bring with, we are aiming to begin, excuse me, with 10 African countries and gradually expand to 30, significantly increasing the availability of data and promoting the exchange of good practices and investment related policies. This initiative also builds on two decades of collaboration between the OECD and pan-African institutions across key policy areas, from productive transformation and domestic resource mobilization to regional value chains and skills development for youth. This work has been carried out in close collaboration with the African Union Commission alongside the OECD Development Centre. At the heart of this partnership lies AVIP. the flagship initiative of our work with the OECD and the African Union, grounded in our 2023 Memorandum of Understanding. It has also been informed by country-driven investment climate reforms, supported through tools such as national investment policy reviews and regional capacity building efforts, in close coordination with African governments and other stakeholders. In closing, please allow me to place momentum of this within the broader OECD effort to boost private investment for development, climate, and biodiversity in emerging and developing economies. This includes our new flagship report, Financing Our Futures, which outlines a pathway to break the mobilization deadlock with specific actions to unlock capital at scale. If you cannot take the money where it is, why do you want to take the money where it is not, which is the poor? That makes common sense to me. So it is going to work. We have to, as the African Union, to get our act together and to be together. We are 54 countries. We are more than one third of the General Assembly. And we have the resources. Actually, as a matter of fact, we are the richest continent in the world, actually. So if we get our act together, if we are determined enough, if we are resilient enough, and if we fight on some of our shortcomings, including corruption, that we have to say too, We will force the rich to pay because they will come to do business because we do have strategic resources that everybody need. So it's about time that we realize that we are very strong when we are together. So yes, we will have to tax the rich because they the one who have the money. So we take the money where it is. Otherwise we don't take the money where it is not among the poor. Thank you.

Thank you so much.

Minister Marcel, what is the importance you give to multilateral agreements, and especially for a fairer taxation system?

Well, Chile has traditionally put multilateralism at the center of everything. We're a small country, so we know that alone we cannot go far. So we have used these initiatives, for example, the OECD, but also the UN. And now we are trying to contribute to these discussions. And I want to highlight something in particular Because when we talk about social covenants and the place that taxation has there, we find another side, which is public expense. And Vitor mentioned a very important case when he referred to that tipping point. That tipping point, Victor, was mentioning has not just to do with taxation, but also with expenditure. Because there are small states that are at risk of being less efficient or less transparent. Because when you're a small state and the demands on the state are not so different, the capacity to sustain expense programs and to apply expenditure according to different programs, then we find more limitations. Small states have to mobilize resources all the time. This works with programs and projects and not with services as such. So this involves higher level of discretion or discretionality, discretion, sorry. So these usually creates a non-ending, a vicious circle, which is difficult to exit. And this is why global agreements are so important. But I don't know how this is in other countries. In Chile, when we have any scandal, any abuse, immediately the public opinion could say, well, this proves that the state is misusing resources. So that's why we shouldn't pay more taxes, right? So I think in this global discussion, if the expenditure is local, it is important to also incorporate this sort of principles. In this sense, we can talk about a social covenant as such. And a social covenant per se doesn't relate just to taxes, but also using those funds properly, those resources we collect. Because we have that obligation to expand them for the benefits of the society, as Ms. Dure was saying. So in this regard, I think there is another angle of this global discussion that we should complement with these principles. I think we should incorporate this to the taxation discussion, yeah. Especially because we are here talking about financing for development, and we sometimes find obstacles for mobilizing resources for international cooperation. And that is domestic resource mobilization. That is the concept. And it is not easier as global cooperation. It requires using those resources, but also managing expenses. So for the global discussion on strengthening the proposals to this level, I think we should also add the thing about using resources properly and about the capacity to sustain public policies, because that makes a difference for the citizenship. These are very relevant components we shouldn't forget about. Thank you so much.

Now, Professor Stiglitz.

I think we can agree that Brazil played a crucial role in 2024 during the G20 presidency, reaching an agreement to push for this agenda, global taxation for this first time. What do you think, what can we expect from this summit and the progress that has been made?

Well, first, let me say, I think there's been a very rich discussion here of both the rationale for why we ought to be taxing the super rich. It's obvious. You don't need to have a Nobel Prize to figure that out. And that, in fact, the world that we have today taxes them at a lower rate than ordinary people, when they should be taxed at a higher rate. So that argument is obvious. The second question often is, why is this a global issue, not just a local issue? And I think the Minister of Finance from Chile brought out one really important aspect of this. It helps create, you might say, global social norms. That was what the SDGs were about, creating global social norms. What is a global social contract, what we should expect in a civilized society. And to me, that's one of the reasons why it's so important that the G20 has taken this up and why it's been taken up here in Seville. But the second reason is that We are part of a global world. The world back when the UK had to deal with Switzerland was just a foreshadowing of what has happened with globalization. We've created tax havens around the world. When I say we've created them, they are the creation of the global community. We could have regulated them. We could have taken other actions. We allow them to exist. And when I say we, why are they there? Well, there are some special interests who benefit from them, and I'll come back to that in a second. So one of the things that is so important about the Seville action platform is that it has concrete measures. And there are lots of concrete measures that can be taken to deal with the tax avoidance that globalization has facilitated. Issues about transparency, issues about global registry, there are many particular things that can be done that actually make, I don't want to say tax avoidance impossible, but at least make it much more difficult. So it's an impediment and makes detection of it easier. Let me before coming to a full answer to your question, point out that while there's been a lot of progress that I'll describe in a second, there are some forces going in the other direction. The first is that globalization has opened up new opportunities for tax avoidance that are just, you know, the tax lawyers we'll find the example of the digital taxes of Apple using Ireland to move all the profits they made in Europe to Ireland. And then using a very special provision of Irish law that said if an Irish subsidiary was controlled from somewhere else, which was Silicon Valley, they didn't have to pay taxes in Ireland. So they moved all their money and said it was due to Ireland, but in Ireland they said it was due to Silicon Valley, and in that way avoided taxes almost completely. So that's the wonders of globalization, but that is what has to be counteracted by specific measures. As I said, there are some, not a surprise, that the people at the top have money to lobby not to be taxed, have money to hire high-priced lawyers to figure out these complexities to avoid tax. When people talk about waste in the government, I look at it systemically. Is that the best use of our talent, to have people figure out how not to pay taxes? The private sector is wasting money. They're hiring from a social point of view. They're wasting money that could have been spent to make sure that people don't die in Africa or in other developing countries on the object simply not paying their fair share of taxes. And that's why this agenda of taxing the super rich is so important. But also, one of the other headwinds that the world is facing right now is Trump. I know one isn't supposed to say that in polite circles, but He's destroyed politeness as even a verb, as a word. So the point I think the rest of the world has to remember is that the US is only 20%, less than 20% of global GDP. Europe as a market is larger than the US. If it doesn't stick together, each country is much smaller. But Europe as a whole is a bigger economy than the US. Why should, in the bargaining about whether Europe should have access to American markets versus America having access to EU markets, why shouldn't the upper hand be in Europe? It's a bigger market. But Europe hasn't acted that way. China stood up. And what we saw when China stood up and said, we're not going to give in, what we saw is what the word, I don't know if many of you know, called taco. Trump always caves in, cops out. So the point is that if Europe stands up, the rest of the world stands up. I think it will make a difference. So let me come to the final part and answer your question. I've been really energized, so optimistic, because of what happened first in the G20 in Brazil, that this issue that we never thought would make the top of the agenda, made onto the agenda. And one of the reasons it made onto the agenda was President Lula was very much aware of the interaction between global social norms and Brazilian social norms, and that putting it on the agenda would actually help the Brazilian agenda. And now I'm actually also so pleased that South Africa has made a commitment to take it up. And then the broad coalition of the willing, almost the entire world with one exception, has gotten together at Seville and made a commitment on this issue. And I have to congratulate Spain for helping engineer this, but it reflects the sentiment of the entire world. I think that's a major step forward. And with the Brazilian, Spanish, and now Chilean, and joining on the Seville Action Platform for dealing with the taxation of the super-rich. I think this provides a kind of momentum going forward after Seville. Here we've been talking about this as a launchpad, and I think it provides a momentum to keep this agenda going forward, which I think is so important. Not because it's just going after social -- taxing the rich in the rich countries, but because countries need the money. The world needs the money in order to address the problem of poverty, health, education, growth in the developing world.

Thank you so much.

My last question is for Susana Ruiz. She has two challenges. First of all, she has to be brief. We are out of time. And then we need a good conclusion. So my question is, can we think about going beyond what we have agreed on this week? Or in other words, if we had another summit in Sevilla in four years, what goals should we discuss?

Well, I want to think this is a starting point, and now we're going to create this action. We're going to have specific goals that will have results. Now we will also have Chile. That's what it seems. So if we have any other delegation that wants to join us, you can come to us. But the only change that will be possible and will make sense is that in a few years, this shouldn't be an initiative led by four or five countries, but it should represent the sentiment and the goodwill of many more countries. Because we can have a space where we discuss about solving global development challenges when we have superpowers that play with our interests but don't pay the taxes they should pay. This has to be a model where we should have more countries on board, but not pressure on unilateralism. We cannot have one country imposing conditions to others. We have to collect the goodwill of all countries. Maybe in three, four years, we hopefully have an agenda with more countries, reflecting a society that will not have just five billionaires that it looks like they can end poverty. That is a bad sign, and I hope that changes in the future, in the next civil summit, because these days, we see the commitment of many countries to give the first steps for example, in Brazil, to move forward. So hopefully, next time, we can celebrate the results moving forward and maybe seeing that this is a reality for a majority of countries. Thank you so much. And if more countries are interested, you can come to us. Thank you.
Well, this is the message we have and we take away. This has been an agile, interesting discussion. Thank you so much for following this session. Thank you.
